utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that -- I find it difficult to guess what the 8 relation with, say, the rule is that you mentioned, but it is a 9 correct statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would presume that, for example, in the case of someone who 11 knew the accused from before the conflict, part of the reason 12 that it is not sensible to seek out minor or peripheral details 13 is that this is a global apprehension process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would not, no, I would not say that. What I would say, 15 this rule is just -- is aimed at two things. One is to just 16 simply save yourself time and to exclude that the witness is 17 talking about someone who simply is totally different from the 18 accused that you have in mind and you want to show in a lineup. 19 The other is that in order to make a proper lineup, you need to 20 have, say, a rough description of, say, what the foils should 21 look like. That is only a rough description. They do not have 22 to have all the same shape of the nose or of the ears. You just 23 want rough categories, like colour of hair, approximate size, 24 colour of skin, something like age. A number of those broad 25 categories is sufficient. So it is very useful to have a 26 description in those terms from the witnesses so that would 27 enable you to make a better lineup. You are also right that it is quite possible that the witness knows a person very well and would still not be able to describe the person, say, in more detail than in those broad categories, because actually he would not be able to, say, well, shape of nose or what colour of eyes or so this person has. So it also would not be extremely useful to ask for more detail in such a description, although if you can get it maybe that can be useful, but this, it does not describe it, say, a witness -- if a witness cannot give such detail. 9 Q. Sure. When we see and recognise someone we know, we do not, if I can use sort of an analogy, record in memory all the specific details of what that person looked like on that particular day or how long his hair was or what clothing he was wearing? 13 A. Right. 14 Q. We record in kind of a visual fashion that was Dr. Wagenaar and we already have the image of that person? 16 A. Right. 17 Q. You have mentioned on other occasions and in some of your works, I take it, that the ability to recognise and remember faces is a rather unique and special human capacity which goes back to the very beginnings of our evolution? 21 A. At least that is the scientific opinion about that specific faculty of human beings. That is, you might even say, a prewired special unit in the brain that has a specific function to recognise faces and nothing else. 25 Q. You also spoke yesterday of one of your rules which -- I am sorry, before I proceed to the rules. I know you spoke about the effect and significance of the four identifications that you have been addressing. You separated those from the recognition witnesses, the 42 or so recognition witnesses. 2 A. Right. 3 Q. On a number of occasions you stressed the significance of the fact that there were four, that although this might seem like a small number, indeed, it was extremely significant, and the reason is that assuming the reliability of the lineup, you do not need more people than that to show that the person selected was at the scene of the crime, is that correct? 9 A. The background of that is that if the only other explanation why they pointed all at the same person is that they guessed, that explanation can already be ruled out when you have four on the basis of the very low probability. 13 Q. Right. In fact, I think you were speaking about four because that was the number in this case. As a matter of fact, you have stated on other occasions that two identifications, given appropriate conditions with the lineup, are sufficient to establish that the person selected was at the scene of the crime? 19 A. Right, and there are two reasons for that. I stated that in the context of Dutch law and, according to Dutch law, just on the basis of, say, legal requirements, two should be enough, but I could also establish that, say, on the basis of probabilities two witnesses, say, in ideal recognition procedures satisfies, say, the sort of statistical requirements that you would want to impose. So there, I would say, statistics and law legislation go very parallel. 27 Q. Yesterday you spoke about the period of time that you felt a witness should or should not be given when viewing a lineup. You mentioned that, in your view, a witness should be given a very specific and limited period of time within which to view the lineup and make a selection. The principle underlying that view, I take it, is that recognition is a relatively fast thing, that it does not require a couple of hours or a couple of days generally, is that right? 7 A. That is correct, yes. 8 Q. So the issue then with this period of time is how long it takes; if it takes too long a period of time, then you become concerned that something other than recognition is going on. It is also true, is it not, that if you insist on a particular length of time that it is going to increase the likelihood that the individual viewing will attempt to conform his selection to that length of time? 15 A. Can you say that again? 16 Q. Sure. If you say to somebody, "Look, you have this amount of time to view the lineup and make a selection", there is a likelihood that the person, that the witness, will make an effort to conform to that period of time, to make a selection within that given period of time? 21 A. Oh, yes, usually witnesses are very co-operative. You give them instructions. They try to follow these instructions -- if that is what you mean, yes. 24 Q. Sure, on the other hand, if you gave someone an unlimited period of time they might take as much time as they felt they needed? 26 A. That is true, the question is, as they need for doing what? 27 Q. That is right. 28 A. Is it as much time as they need for, say, a proper recognition, 1 or is it as much time as they need for a rather complicated 2 process of reasoning or deduction where they try to deduce who 3 is the target instead of, say, simply recognising him? But you 4 are quite right; if you give them an unlimited amount of time 5 they can start using that time for, well, we do not know exactly 6 what. That is exactly why you do not want to give them 7 unlimited amounts of time, because you want to control that they 8 are involving themselves in a recognition process and not in the 9 process of logical deduction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But giving someone an unlimited amount of time gives you an 11 opportunity to see how much time that person may really have 12 needed to make a selection? On the other hand, insisting that 13 someone conformed to a particular amount of time may compel that 14 person to make his selection faster than he otherwise would 15 have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, you are quite right that if you would measure the 17 time, that would give you an extra piece of information if you 18 record it properly. The thing is, however, that in the 19 way identification procedures are defined, there is no rule for 20 how we would use, say, that extra piece of information. For 21 instance, when it runs -- to give the worst example -- counter, 22 say, to verbal expression, how we are going to use that. The 23 witness points at one, but then the witness spends an extremely 24 long time at another picture, what does that mean? It leads to 25 all sorts of uncertainties of interpretation. We have had many examples where it was argued, "Well, 27 the witness said this, but she spent so much time looking at 28 this picture, she must also have recognised that person". That introduces all kinds of uncertainties that, say, a proper test should not have. Therefore, in my opinion, it is better to have strict rules to predefine exactly what is a positive identification and what is not, and that sort of excludes also the difficult discussions later on. 6 Q. In any event, that particular instruction is not particularly relevant if the viewing and recognition is all done quickly? 8 A. No, if the whole process is rather quick, like I read in one of the witnesses said, "Well, the whole going through the book is finished in a few minutes", that is a rather quick process. That does not -- it would not run counter to, say, my rules or recommendations, so I would not see any difficulty, a special difficulty, there. The question remains, of course, of how the pacing exactly was, because even within a process of several minutes you can show one picture a bit longer than the others. But, say, if the whole process took in the order of minutes, I would say that there is no question of excessive time and eliciting reasoning processes. What I would rather like to prevent is the process of hours. 21 Q. I want to speak with you also about the view that you expressed about selecting or about the instruction to a witness to select just one photo in a body lineup, just one person. As you discussed yesterday, that obviates the problem that might arise if someone selected more than one? 26 A. Yes. 27 Q. At the same time, if a witness went through the lineup and thought he recognised more than one person, in the face of that instruction, that witness would then select just one person, is that not right? 3 A. Can you say that again? 4 Q. Sure. 5 A. I am not exactly certain what you are saying. 6 Q. That instruction tells a witness that he should just select one photograph, although it may be the case that the witness believes he recognises two photographs or even three photographs in the lineup? 10 A. In principle, that would hardly be possible if the witness is instructed to see whether a certain person known to the witness by name or not by name, but a certain person that the witness has seen, has met, at the scene of the crime, to see whether that person is in the lineup, it is still possible that the subject -- that the witness would say, "Well, there are two pictures of the same person in the lineup; he appears twice", but that rarely happens because the pictures are clearly representing different people. In that case, the witness can only identify no one or one, but not logically two. The problem occurs only if you instruct the witness whether he or she can recognise anybody, because then it is quite likely or quite possible that the subject says, "Well, I recognise this person. This is the man I discussed, say, about the crime, but I recognise several others as well". So that instruction to recognise, whether you can recognise anybody, is sort of inviting this problem and is, therefore, not recommended. You exclude that problem if you say in this particular case, "Well, we have talked about Mr. Tadic. Let us look. Is the Mr. Tadic that you have seen, is he among the persons that I am going to show you?" Then logically, I would say, the witness can either indicate no one or one. 5 Q. But the problem that you are attempting to eliminate with that instruction is one which does not work to the credit of the witness in selecting the accused's photograph? 8 A. Can you expand on that? I think my language facility ..... 9 Q. If the witness selects the accused's photograph and also selects some of the foils ---- 11 A. Yes. 12 Q. --- as being people he recognises, you have additional information which might assist you in gauging the weight to be given the selection of the accused's photograph? 15 A. You might, but you do not know what information you have, because if you allow a witness to point at several people and the witness is, in fact, guessing, then you increase the guessing level and you do not know what the weight of the test is any more. That is why you should not do that. Sure, if the witness is truly recognising various people, you get information about whom they recognised. But if the witness is guessing, the likelihood of, say, guessing correctly, guessing correctly who the accused is, is increased, and that is exactly what the test is for, to eliminate those people who really do not have a clear image of the perpetrator and are guessing. That is why you have the foils, to exclude guessing. So if you do not assume a person is guessing, well, it is not worth doing the test anyway. 1 Q. But allowing person to select more photographs elicits the information that the person is guessing and provides additional information? 4 A. No, no, no, it is not even that and definitely not in your case where it is logically possible that they recognise some of the others, because the others are people from the former Republic of Yugoslavia, and we have no way of knowing whether they know these people or not. No, you really are asking for troubles. You increase the guessing level too and unknown -- with an unknown amount; whereas the set up of the test is such that you kept the guessing level very low at 1/13 which is extremely good. So I would say if you have such an extensive test with 12 foils, and you took all the care to make certain that these are not people known to the witnesses, you sort of spoil your own test by after that allowing the subject to point at more people. What if they point at all 13, they say, "I know them all"? Would you say, "Ah, the witness identified Mr. Tadic"? 19 Q. That is right, then you have additional information with which to gauge the reliability of the witness's selection? 21 A. No, I would say you have no additional information. You have lost a witness, because you do not know what the identification means any more. 24 Q. Yes, that is exactly right. It does not prejudice the accused; it works to his advantage? 26 A. I think we are here stumbling over a thing that might be different between your culture and my culture. I am not used to think in whose advantage it is. I am used to think in terms of how close can we get to the truth. So I would not run tests that make it extremely easy for an accused to get off, to get off. I would try to organise tests that help us to find out whether the accused is the same as the perpetrator or not. To that purpose, I would say, you need to ask the witnesses to indicate one person or no one, but never two, three or four. 7 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Let me ask you this, if I may just interrupt one moment, in terms of searching for the truth, but if the witness who is looking at the foils admits that he knows all of the individuals and, even though he knows them all, he is able to select the alleged perpetrator, is that not of assistance in determining the truth, that is, the ability of the witness to identify the perpetrator, and does that not take into account the possibility that he may, having known someone, place that person in his memory as being at the scene? 16 A. I think you are quite right, your Honour, if you would ask a witness, "Well, even if you know them all, who of these people is the Mr. Tadic you are talking about?" 19 Q. Yes. 20 A. Ask specifically, "Even if you know them all, we are not so much interested, now we want to know of you whom of these 13 is Mr. Tadic". In fact, then, of course, you are asking the same question that I proposed and that I proposed you asked in the beginning: "You have talked about Mr. Tadic. Is one of these people the Mr. Tadic you were talking about?" After that you can also ask (and it does not invalid, say, the earlier identification), "And do you happen to know some of the others?" There is no problem there. But if you just allow them to point at an unlimited number of people and say, "Well, he might be someone I saw and he might be someone I saw", and you do not identify whom of these people is the Mr. Tadic he saw, then you are lost. 5 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Excuse me. 6 MR. TIEGER: In any event, doctor, if the witness looks at the lineup and says, "That person is Mr. Tadic" or "That person is the one who beat me on this occasion" ---- 9 A. Right. 10 Q. --- then the problem is ----- 11 A. "But, by the way, I also know some of the others", no problem there, as long as there is only one chance given to identify whom of these people Mr. Tadic is. If they say, "This is Mr. Tadic, but he also looks a bit like Mr. Tadic, maybe it is him", then you are lost. Then you have two shots instead of one. 17 Q. You discussed the question of reporting negative results or misses, and whether or not those might have some diagnostic significance. I believe you indicated, for example, that a negative result could be interesting or not. For example, if you know that the person viewing a lineup was 300 or 400 metres away from the incident, the fact that there is a negative result is uninteresting? 24 A. Correct. 25 Q. Then, I suppose, that would be true for a variety of similar circumstances if the person was not paying attention or was not ---- 28 A. It was very dark or something was blocking the view or the person was turned around to the other way so they only saw the back of them; all sorts of reasons, yes. 3 Q. Even for reasons unrelated to circumstances but more related to human memory, I presume that a certain number of misses are also expected? 6 A. Oh, definitely, recognition is not always perfect. Even some people who have closely watched a scene might made a mistake, but if they make such statements like, "I will never forget that face, I see that every night in my dreams" or so, and then they cannot recognise, I think in that case you should interpret the negative outcome as meaning that the accused is the wrong person. 13 Q. It is a matter of assessing all the circumstances? 14 A. Right, yes. 15 Q. You point out ---- 16 A. I only wanted to say that negative results can be very valid and diagnostic information. 18 Q. In terms of numbers, for example, you indicated yesterday that it could be significant if a lineup was shown to 50 people only four identified the accused. You are nodding so the answer to that is "yes"? 22 A. Yes. 23 Q. Of course, that would also depend on the circumstances surrounding the viewing of the incident by the other 46? 25 A. Yes, so what you would need to know about the 46, is there good explanation why they failed or is there no good explanation and should you know assume that this is just representing the guessing level? That is why you have to look closely at them. You do not have just to know the number, you have to look at the conditions as well. 3 Q. But, in any event, those kinds of numbers would cause you some concern? 5 A. If they were as large as that, yes, I think that would cause me great concern. 7 Q. What if a lineup was shown to 10 people and seven or eight selected the accused? 9 A. I do not think it would be very wise for me to make assessments of, say, various amounts and say, "Well, this is all right, this is marginal, this is whatever", because it all depends on the circumstances. The only thing I wanted to stress is you have to know about these others. Even if there is only one other, I think the Court ought to know about it because it can be very diagnostic. 16 Q. You spoke yesterday about a lineup which was prepared by German law enforcement authorities, the one that you viewed. 18 A. I saw it for the first time yesterday, yes. 19 Q. OK. I know you were asked a number of questions about the possible effects of seeing such a lineup. None of the four people that you were talking about, that is, the four identification witnesses in this case were shown that lineup, as far as you know? 24 A. That is good -- well, I do not know about that, but if you say that, I would say that is good. 26 Q. Fine. You are not aware of it? 27 A. No, no, I am not aware of it. I have no knowledge about it. 28 Q. OK. 1 A. I think you know very well what they were shown. 2 Q. OK. 3 A. So if you say so that they did not see that, I would say that is good. 5 Q. So it is irrelevant to them? 6 A. The existence of that lineup if they have not seen it, they have not -- there is no possible way they could have seen it, I would say it does not bear on that case. 9 Q. If someone who knew Mr. Tadic from before the war was shown that lineup and selected him from that, there is nothing wrong with that either, as far as you are concerned? 12 A. If they really knew him well before the war, there is nothing that you are going to show them that would, sort of, interfere with, say, their intimate knowledge that they are having anyway. 15 Q. You would be completely comfortable with the German authorities showing such a witness, someone who knew him from before the war, a single photograph of Mr. Tadic to say, "Is that the ---- 18 A. Yes, because ---- 19 Q. --- "man?" 20 A. --- well, the reason is, of course, because their recognition, by definition, does not have, say, on logical grounds the power to place Mr. Tadic at the scene of the crime because they are going to recognise him anyway, whether they saw him at the scene of the crime or not. So, since the power of that testimony or, you might probably go, the probative value of that testimony is much more limited, you do not have to provide very difficult, intricate tests. It does not mean anything to them. 28 Q. So the German lineup would be irrelevant for diagnostic purposes 1 to that group as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To that group of the people who knew him really well, I would 3 say it is irrelevant. Now, I am not -- maybe I should qualify 4 that a little bit. I have read in the various testimonies that 5 some of them, some of these witnesses, know him very, very 6 well. They went to the same school. They knew him from his 7 birth. They were his teachers and so on. They knew him on a 8 daily basis. Some of them knew him a little bit less intimate, 9 knew who he was, had seen him in the village a number of times 10 or he was pointed out to them. There is a range of acquaintance there. Of course, 12 that range may include some people who really did not remember 13 his face quite well. For those few, the presenting of 14 photographs may have had the effect of, sort of, refreshing 15 their memory, so it would have mattered. But I have no clear 16 opinion about that, because I find it not easy to make an 17 assessment on the basis of the various testimonies what the 18 exact range is. I know that many of the subjects knew him extremely 20 well. They knew him on a day-to-day basis. I would say, to 21 them, it does not matter what kind of photograph you show. But 22 there might be a few on the other end of the range where you may 23 have some doubts, whether, say, showing of pictures later on may 24 have, sort of, refreshed or altered their memory, but I do not 25 think that many of them. But I must warn you, of course, that 26 my little table that just classifies witnesses in groups is a 27 little bit artificial. There is a range, say, within the cells 28 of that table. 1 Q. Yesterday you mentioned that there was no linear relationship between the number of witnesses who identify and the extent of probative value. Were you referring when you said that only to the issue of identification and selection from a lineup rather than recognition witnesses? 6 A. Well, I think that the statement is meant for the true identification witnesses because, logically, for the recognition witnesses there would be no relationship at all because the probative value of their recognition for placing someone at the scene of the crime is low anyway. But since the others, the four, in our case, are so important, there I think it is useful to warn that 40 is not extremely better, much better, than just four, because if you assume that those four, although they identified, could have made a mistake, then the basis of that mistake, for instance, the very close resemblance between the accused and another true perpetrator, for instance, like twin brothers, if you are afraid that would have caused the mistake, you can be almost certain that you are going to prolong the mistake and repeat the mistake with other subjects, and that is "more subjects than" does not help. If you are afraid about, say, the guessing level, then four is already enough. It does not help to get to even lower probabilities. 23 Q. I believe I understood that. I just wanted to clarify that you were talking about identifications and not talking about the recognition witnesses. 26 A. There is, of course, if I may add a remark, if you have witnesses who have witnessed different crimes or describing different scenes, they were not all, say, like all 52, witness to the same crime, then it could be important to have a few witnesses for each separate crime, of course. 3 Q. Yes, that is a matter of common sense? 4 A. But that is a matter of sheer logic. 5 Q. Right. We talked about the Doob & Kirshenbaum test yesterday at some length. That is a test which is performed by people in your field and which you performed to determine whether or not the photospread is suggestive or not? 9 A. Yes, that is correct. 10 Q. That test was administered in this case to 39 subjects? 11 A. That is right. 12 Q. In fact, actually I guess that would be 40 since you also made an effort to identify the ---- 14 A. Oh, yes, but that is not in the report -- only the 39 count. 15 Q. OK, but you also tried to pick out the photograph of the person you thought might be the accused when you did not know who he was? 18 A. I always try -- I am always the first subject in my own experiments, but I do not count that. 20 Q. OK. You picked out one of the foils? 21 A. I did, yes. 22 Q. After you completed or perhaps during the process of performing the Doob & Kirschenbaum test you began to wonder whether or not former residents of Yugoslavia could distinguish Serbs from Muslims from Croats and so on, and wondered whether or not Mr. Tadic was the only Serb and so that you performed an experiment in Belgrade ---- 28 A. That is correct, yes. 1 Q. --- and found that the subjects there, who were more or less representative of the witness population here, found it impossible to classify the pictures according to ethnic background? 5 A. Yes. 6 Q. That indicated that the hypothetical problem that had concerned you did not seem to exist and had not occurred? 8 A. Yes, with the one small proviso that I made yesterday, provided that, say, the faces that they saw indeed belonged to the category of people living in the former Republic of Yugoslavia. But I must say I was quite reassured after seeing those results that nothing had gone grossly wrong in the selection of the foils, yes. 14 Q. What question did you pose to the subjects in that Belgrade experiment? 16 A. The question was, "We are going to show you a number of pictures. Here are a number of categories that you could insert them in, like Croat, Macedonian, Montenegrin and so on. Will you try to make a judgment or, if you cannot make a judgment, to just guess to which category these people shown in the photographs belong". So is a kind of what we call a forced choice test. They have to categorise everybody, even if they are totally uncertain, to make sure that if they do not think they can but, in fact, they can, but they are not aware of their abilities, that would come out if you forced them to guess. So, if you force them to guess and even then they cannot do it, you can be sure there is no, say, conscious ability to do it but also not an unconscious ability to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any reason why you did not put in a photograph of 2 someone or some photographs of people known to be from the 3 former Yugoslavia to see whether or not the subjects could do 4 that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, there was a very clear reason. We, sort of, spent the 6 whole summer of getting good pictures of people having lived in 7 the former Yugoslavia, and that appeared to be extremely 8 difficult. We also spent a lot of time in finding subjects from 9 the former Yugoslavia which appeared to be extremely difficult. 10 Only when, say, the date of this hearing came closer, I realised 11 that I would not want to sit here and have to tell the Court 12 that I had no information about this problem. So what I did is I contacted a number of colleagues in 14 universities in the former Republic, to ask them whether they if 15 we came over for two days could provide the subjects to us. 16 They all responded positively. The University of Belgrade was 17 the only one that opened before 1st October. In the other there 18 were no students available before 1st October, so we selected 19 Belgrade for that. But at that moment there was no time to 20 produce new pictures, so we used the 12 pictures, the 12 foils 21 in the test that you had used. I thought that was appropriate 22 because the true question is about these pictures not about 23 others. So, I thought if we know about these pictures, that 24 they cannot easily be recognised as Serbs or non-Serbs or 25 whatever, I would feel quite sure that the test itself had not 26 gone wrong. What you proposed to do with these other pictures is 28 something that I would also have liked to do, but that should not have prevented me doing the test with the real foils because that is the thing that really matters. 3 Q. I take it that nothing that happened during the course of this experiment or any other review you did would cause you now to advise big city police departments that they should check to see whether the accused is Jewish or Italian and whether the photographs are ..... 8 A. No. No. 9 Q. In any event, your concern would be entirely alleviated, I take it, if you found that eight or nine of the photographs of the foils were persons from former Yugoslavia? 12 A. Sure, the rule that I used myself was that there should at least be five foils that are good representatives of, say, the group to which the accused belongs. So if you have five of those, five or six, I would say there is a sufficient number of alternatives that, say, a guessing witness I could have used to guess at. 18 Q. By the way, I should probably clarify the chronology that led to this since it was discussed a bit yesterday. In your letter to the Prosecution after performing the Doob & Kirshenbaum test, you mentioned in one section something about this. What you said was, "If it is argued before the Tribunal that Dutch subjects have insufficient ability to distinguish the various ethnic groups, then such a test might be performed." 25 A. Yes. 26 Q. We discussed it and I told you that I could not see any basis for that being argued since everyone from former Yugoslavia said that that kind of distinction was not made and not possible to make. 2 A. Yes, which, of course, leads us to the problem which was mentioned yesterday, that people do not always know what abilities they have. There are some things that we can do we do not even know we can do. You would be very surprised to see. 6 Q. Except in this case we know now ---- 7 A. Yes. 8 Q. --- but, in any event, that ended the matter for our purposes? 9 A. For your purposes it did, for mine it did not. So I wanted to run that test to really see. 11 Q. Just to clarify, you did not insist to me that I should get for you the information about who the foils were? 13 A. No, I pointed out what the problem was to you and it is completely up to you to follow that up or not. 15 Q. OK. You also did not advise me when you began embarking on the test with the Yugoslav subjects on behalf of the Defence? 17 A. No, I think the first test that you do is to do it with Dutch subjects because, for instance, there are a number of things in a test that are possibly suggestive and that would be suggestive to any subjects. For instance, to take a gross area, if one of the picture is larger, that would influence all subjects, no matter where they come from. So to detect, say, a number of those problems in the photospread that have nothing to do with ethnic groups, Dutch subjects would be quite sufficient and, of course, you would first take this first, this very easy step of testing Dutch subjects. It does not exclude this one single point of ethnicity, but it already excludes a number of other mistakes that could be present in the photospread. 1 Q. I understand that. I was just asking you whether or not you advised me when you began performing the test with the Yugoslav subjects, and you did not, correct? 4 A. No. I reported, say, what they did and what they did not do. It made sure that all sort of other mistakes were not in the spread, but there is a question mark with respect to ethnicity. I just mentioned it to you that that might be a problem. The problem was big enough -- and we have discussed that -- it was big enough for me to try to go on and find out for myself because I do not like to come to Court and have to say, "Well, I do not know that. I could have done it but I did not". So I have advised you that I would try to go on and investigate this on my own. 14 Q. You were working with the Defence about that time, were you not? 15 A. I am not working with -- I am working with you trying to answer your questions. I tried to answer questions of the Defence. I am not working with the Defence in the sense that -- in the meaning that it might have in your country. 19 Q. I was ---- 20 A. I am not taking sides or anything with the Defence. 21 Q. --- not asking you that question, doctor. I just wanted to know the chronology of everyone's involvement. 23 A. Or just to prevent any misunderstandings because we all come from different countries and, say, that statement might mean different things to different people. 26 Q. Let me ask you something about your field of study, experimental psychology. You referred, for example, to experimental data and empirical data on which you rely. I take it by that you mean experiments which are devised by people in your field to test certain theories. It is correct to say that these tests have been criticised as not reflecting real life conditions? 4 A. Well, not all empirical data on which my insights are based are, say, laboratory tests. I also published the results of many case studies in which identification was at issue. I even published statistics across a number of such case studies and I am not the only one. That is quite usual in my field. There is a concern about experiments, because reality is usually always one step more complicated than, say, what we try to create in the laboratory. 12 Q. (To the witness): You may answer the question. 28 THE WITNESS: I think we should make a clear distinction between two 1 situations. One is the situation in which the witness saw 2 someone commit a crime or just saw someone, and that was the 3 first time that the witness sees this person. So it is the 4 first impression of a certain person. So that is not a 5 recognition because it is the first encounter. It is the sort 6 of imprinting the image of a person you did not know yet. Fleeting glance, technically, usually is referring to 8 this situation, because if in that situation you see a person 9 for a very short period, you might not receive a good enough 10 impression of that person to be able to recognise that person 11 later. For instance, in British law fleeting glances during the 12 first encounter, sort of, rule out identification tests, because 13 the first impression cannot have been good enough. I think your question refers to the second situation 15 where now the witness is asked to recognise a person, so that is 16 possibly the second encounter -- that is what you want to know, 17 is this the second encounter or not -- and recognition, 18 recognising a person whom you have encountered before can go 19 much quicker. It can be within the second that you say, "Ah, 20 ha, that is him". So, for a recognition, say, a very short 21 presentation should not rule out the acceptability of the 22 response of the witness. On the contrary, if the witness would 23 need a very long time you would say, "Ah, ha, but that cannot be 24 a recognition because recognitions usually go very quick". So, the presentation time for the second situation, 26 the recognition situation, need not be very long, whereas for 27 the first situation you may require that it is reasonably long, 28 long enough to form a good impression of a person. Now, if your question is how much time do you need for a recognition, what is a reasonable presentation time, I think I have to repeat my answer. Anything between zero seconds and half a minute would be totally acceptable for recognition. If a witness needs more than half a minute to recognise a person, you may doubt whether that is a true recognition. 7 Q. Thank you. 8 A. But if a witness after two second says, "That's him", I would say that is totally acceptable. 10 Q. Thank you. Another matter I want to clarify is the German photospread that was shown to you yesterday. Again, to be absolutely certain about this, would it be relevant if the four witnesses you mentioned yesterday and today, the four witnesses we all focused on, had been involved in a German photospread, in this German photospread? 16 A. Yes, then, say, the photospread, the 13-person photospread that was reported in the records, would be a repeated test, and it is not certain any more why they recognise the face because they have seen this person at the scene of the crime or in a previous test. So that would be extremely relevant, yes. 21 Q. Thank you. You were also asked questions by the Prosecution about the instruction. Am I right in thinking that it all comes down to two issues, whether the instruction is open or whether the instruction is more precisely formulated? Yes, or some -- simply it is even -- the risk is even bigger. 1 What if they try to recognise, say, a limited set of people that 2 they have in mind and do not realise that maybe someone out of 3 that, outside that set, could be present? Then they are not 4 even telling, maybe not even telling you that the one person you 5 are interested in is in the set. So you really run a risk on 6 all sides. It might be that the witness is telling you far more 8 than you want to know and you cannot interpret it any more. It 9 is also possible that the witness is exactly not telling you 10 what you want to know, although the witness could easily have 11 done that and you just miss information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Theoretically, you might have two situations here. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is very difficult then to give a correct instruction 20 because the correct instruction mentions, say, one particular 21 figure that needs to be identified. Also, it would be rather 22 difficult because, ideally, you would first ask the witness to 23 describe that person. In some conditions, you then have to stop 24 because you have to construct the test on the basis of that 25 description. So, if the first thing that you want to do in the 27 encounter with the witness is use the photo test, then that 28 photo test would logically not be based on any descriptions that 1 the witness gave. So you are already in trouble. No, the logical way of doing it is interview the 3 witness, asking the subject -- asking the witness to describe 4 the person, say, that might be present in the test, and then ask 5 the subject, "Well, this particular person that you described to 6 me, is he present in this photo parade or live parade or not?"

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What if the test was run and afterwards a description was asked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, then you run a great risk. You first present the test. 9 It is possible that -- let me give you an example, a very simple 10 example. You have constructed a test. All foils really look 11 like -- look like the accused, so it seems to be an unbiased 12 test. But now the witness says, "Ah, but the person I saw had a 13 little scar just under the eyes", and if you look well you can 14 see the accused has that and the others have not. Well, once the witness has that information but you 16 did not know because you first applied the test, it is, of 17 course, extremely easy for the witness to identify the one 18 person because that one person has the scar and the others have 19 not. In that sense, given that piece of information is not a 20 fair test any more. So you first want to know what is the 21 information that the witness already has, and can we find foils 22 that, sort of, show all these characteristics that were 23 presented by the witness? Now, that might happen, so you run a great risk. It 25 might be all right because the witness is not giving you any 26 more details that now invalidate the test, but since you do not 27 want to run that risk, I would say, first, you ask for a 28 description, then you look at the test and say, "Would this test be a fair test for this witness?" Then you go on. Let me give you an example. We have had in Netherlands the rather famous case of the killings in a supermarket in Oosterbuk Albert Heijn supermarket. In that case we had to construct, because the witnesses gave different amounts of detail, different lineups for all subjects, for all witnesses. There you simply could not use the same live lineup for every witness. So, first, you have to ask their descriptions, then you construct the lineups. 10 Q. Thank you. Would that mean that the records of the test should place the test in sequence with the interview? So if we only have the record of the test itself, should we also not know when the test was run during or after the interview or at what stage of the interview and when the description was given by the witness, should that be indicated? 16 A. Yes, I think so. 17 Q. Thank you. You also testified this morning again about the Belgrade experiment. Why did you run that experiment? Was that on the request of the Defence? 20 A. No, I just ran it -- I informed both Prosecution and the Defence that I was worried about this detail and that I would try to run an experiment on this, just to be sure about this detail, but we run it on our own initiative. No one requested it. 24 Q. You testified also that the subjects with whom you ran the test were students from the Belgrade University, is that right? 26 A. That is correct, yes. 27 Q.
