That removed me from the room, but if it was something that was blanked out in his mind, I asked Pero Opacic if he could just talk to him and, perhaps, stimulate something in his mind, to say something that he may remember that only those two had done, perhaps a football game, perhaps a birthday party or something that may stimulate something. That was done. After some time, I think probably 20 to 25 minutes, I went back into the room with the interpreter and I said, "Has anything been resolved?" or words that effect, "Has anything been resolved?" and he said, "Yes, this is (redacted)". He said, "Yes, (redacted), Janko Opacic, and (redacted) (redacted) Pero". 25 Q. What did he say to you then after he told you this? 26 A. Well, at that time I went and got Miss de Bertodano and Mr. Petrovic. They came back to the room with me and I confirmed that again in their presence and then we all left the room. 2 Q. What was the next thing to occur? 3 A. I then went back to the room with the interpreter at about 12.30 p.m. and I again had a conversation with (redacted). The first thing I asked him was why he had lied about the death of (redacted), and why he refused to acknowledge photographs that were put to him in the Court as (redacted). He apologised and he told me that he had something to tell me. He then stated he had been set up by the "Bosnians". He said that after he had been captured -- when he was captured in about November 1994 he was shot. He was captured as a member of the Serb Army and at that time he was interviewed by the military, and he had been beaten by the interrogators. 14 Q. Did you understand what he meant by the "Bosnians"? 15 A. By the Bosnian government authorities, and at that time I believe it would be, my understanding is that it is the Bosnian government military, the army of the Bosnian -- Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. 19 Q. Thank you. Go on. 20 A. He stated that he was told that he had been in the camp by the interrogators, and that he did, in fact, know Dusko Tadic, I then asked him if he, in fact, did know Tadic and he stated that the first time he had seen Tadic was on a video shown to him (redacted). I understand that to be when he was transferred from military custody into civilian police custody. 26 Q. He did not indicate to you who showed him this video? 27 A. No, he has indicated a certain person whose name I cannot recollect at the moment, but I do have in some records and I am 1 attempting to find that out now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that after his initial interview by the military, he was 4 transferred (redacted) where he spoke with police interrogators 5 for seven hours a day for about one month. The purpose of these 6 conversations was to train Witness L -- (redacted), I am 7 sorry, to give evidence against Dusko Tadic. The training took the form of watching videos of 9 Mr. Tadic and watching videos of the Trnopolje camp. He said 10 that after that training was complete, he then took part in the 11 taking of a statement that was signed by him. I then asked him was he actually a guard at the camp 13 and he told me that he never was. I asked him how he knew the 14 layout of the camp and the surrounding areas so well. He stated 15 that he used to play football with his friends, and sometimes 16 (redacted) (when (redacted) was not at the front fighting in the war) 17 within the grounds of the camp. He also stated that he used to 18 pass the camp on occasions and saw detainees within the camp. I then asked him why he had pleaded guilty to 20 something that he had never done. He stated that he had been 21 threatened that if he did not co-operate with the Bosnian 22 authorities he would be executed, and I took this to mean that 23 he would be murdered as opposed to an execution by a lawful 24 court order. I then asked him about the identification of (redacted) 26 (redacted) that he related to the Bosnian 27 authorities, and he stated that they had told him that (redacted) 28 (redacted) had worked with him in the camp, and once he had got that knowledge, to protect (redacted), he told them that (redacted) was dead. 3 Q. In relation to these matters that have just come to light, have you had an opportunity to do any further investigations? 5 A. No, not at this stage, not as a result of what has occurred today, no. 7 MR. NIEMANN: No further questions of the witness, your Honour. 8 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 10 Q. Just one matter and that is if you can help me with this matter, Mr. Reid? Do you know how it was that Witness L, (redacted), came about to become a witness in these proceedings? 13 A. Yes, the Tribunal was contacted, or the investigation section at the Office of the Prosecutor was contacted, I think, in March 1995 that there was a potential witness in relation to the trial of Mr. Tadic. I travelled (redacted), I think, in April 1995 and had an initial interview with him. 18 Q. Which body or organisation provided the contact with this witness? 20 A. It is the investigation department of the Bosnian government, the police investigation department. 22 MR. KAY: Thank you very much. That is all I ask. 23 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Niemann, do you have additional questions? 24 MR. NIEMANN: I have nothing further, your Honour. 25 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Is there any objection to Mr. Reid being permanently excused? I ask that question each time and, of course, Mr. Reid is with the Prosecutor's Office, but it has become routine. 1 MR. KAY: I think, as the officer in the case, he will probably be staying with it anyway, your Honour, so I am not sure anyone really wants him released. 4 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Very good. Then you will around, will you not, Mr. Reid ---- 6 A. I will your Honour, yes. 7 Q. --- until we finish the case, in case you are asked to return to give testimony by counsel or by the Trial Chamber? 9 A. Yes. 10 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: So you are now excused. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 13 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Kay, would you call your next witness, please? 15 MR. KAY: Your Honour, we call the accused Dusko Tadic. MR. DUSKO TADIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 18 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Sir, would you please take the oath that is being handed to you? 20 THE WITNESS [In translation]: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 23 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Very good. Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Kay, you may begin. 25 MR. KAY: Thank you, your Honour. 26 Q. Can you give the Court your full name, please? 27 A. Dusko Tadic. 28 Q. What is your date of birth? 1 A. October 1st 1955 in Kozarac. 2 Q. Is your father or was your father called Ostoja Tadic? 3 A. Yes. 4 Q. What is your mother's name? 5 A. My mother's name is Staka. 6 Q. Do you have brothers Mladen, Stojan and Ljubo? 7 A. Yes. 8 Q. Is it right that your brother Ljubo gave evidence in these proceedings recently? 10 A. Yes, his real name is Ljubomir. 11 Q. Thank you. Were you brought up in Kozarac and was that the place of your family home? 13 A. Yes, I was born in Kozarac, like my other brothers, and that is where I lived. 15 Q. Can you tell us what your education was? Were you educated in the local school? 17 A. Yes, I completed elementary school in Kozarac, like all my other brothers. After elementary school, I continued my education in Belgrade where I completed my secondary schooling. 20 Q. Do you have any academic or other qualifications for trades? 21 A. Yes, I completed secondary school for TV mechanics in Belgrade, a technical school. 23 Q. When you left school what was your first job? 24 A. I first started working in Cajavec, the company Cajavec, in Banja Luka. That was at the beginning of 1981, I think. 26 Q. Is that an electrical company? 27 A. Yes, it is an electrical company, a well-known firm manufacturing TV sets. I think it is the only such factory in Bosnia-Herzegovina. 2 Q. For how long did you work there? 3 A. I worked until 1984 or '85. 4 Q. What was your next job, having finished work at that factory? 5 A. My next job was private business. Around 1987 I opened a private company in Croatia in the town of Sisak, and I worked with that firm until 1989, in various parts of Yugoslavia, but it was registered in Sisak. 9 Q. Did you have a partner in that business? 10 A. Yes, my partner was my long-standing friend, Solkonovic Fikret, and while we were working in the territory of Croatia and Slovenia, and afterwards another friend joined us from Kozarac, but he was not an official partner. 14 Q. In between those last two jobs you have told us about, did you work in Libya or did you go to Libya and stay there for some time? 17 A. Yes, I think this was in '85 or '86. Actually, I spent up to six or seven months there. 19 Q. What was the reason for going to Libya? 20 A. The main reasons were economic problems in former Yugoslavia. Life was getting difficult. Some people were doing well, but we always wanted to do better. 23 Q. Did you get any work in Libya? 24 A. No, my wife got a job as a nurse, so I left with my daughter. I hoped to get a job but that did not happen. 26 Q. You have told us about your wife. When were you married? 27 A. I was married in 1979, but officially we were not married. Only after our first daughter was born we actually got married. 1 Q. How many children did you have within that marriage? 2 A. My oldest daughter is called Valentina. She was born on 11th April, 1981. The younger daughter's name is Aleksandra, 4th March 1989 is her date of birth. The older one was born in Banja Luka and the younger one in Prijedor. 6 Q. Did there come a stage when you and your wife went through divorce procedures? 8 A. Yes, upon our return from Libya we agreed to divorce and we did, me and my wife, and this lasted for quite some time. Actually, we never got officially remarried again, but this was something that never really concerned us. We did not care much about it, the actual official marriage or divorce but when we lived together. 14 Q. What was the reason for having that divorce? 15 A. As I said, from the first day I wanted to go abroad and upon return from Libya I did not have a job. We had no livelihood from friends from -- some friends from Switzerland promised to find a job for us and that it would be much easier if we were divorced. First of all, my wife is a nurse, a medical nurse, and for medical staff it was quite easy to find jobs abroad if they were divorced, and that is the only reason for our divorce. 22 Q. So was your wife trying to find employment abroad that would have been easier for her to obtain if she did not have officially a husband? 25 A. Yes, yes, that was just the -- you had to provide a document certifying that you were not married. 27 Q. Throughout your marriage has that been the main occupation of your wife, working as a nurse? 1 A. Yes, she graduated secondary medical school, I think it was called Maglajic in Banja Luka, and she worked in that profession all her life. 4 Q. Did she work in hospitals around Kozarac? Can you tell us which hospitals she worked in? 6 A. From 1980 she worked in Kozarac. At that time she had -- the place where she was working was a health centre, though it belonged administratively to the Prijedor hospital. She worked in Kozarac, then for a time after that in an outpost in the village of Kozarusa, and occasionally she would work at the outpatients clinic in Trnopolje. Then for a time she would be a visiting nurse on the territory of Kozarac. These were mostly the jobs she had until she left Kozarac in April 1992. 14 Q. At some stage after April 1992 did she resume her nursing work in Prijedor? 16 A. Yes, she started working. I think it was August 1992. She also worked in the Prijedor health centre. It is, so to speak, the same institution only located in Prijedor because there was no such post any more in Kozarac. 20 Q. We have heard about your family. Were you a close family, a family that had good relations amongst you, sons, with your parents? 23 A. Mostly, yes. Nothing special, there is nothing special to be said about that. When we were younger, of course, we were extremely close but as we grew up, since there was a considerable difference between me and my eldest brother -- my eldest brother is nine years older than me -- we were not so close because of this large difference. As we grew up and were ready for secondary school, some went on to higher schools. Most of my brothers left Kozarac for their education. Then they went to Banja Luka, Belgrade, and so on. 4 Q. We have heard that your eldest brother, Stojan, travelled around the former Yugoslavia and was in business, is that right? 6 A. Yes, for a time he worked in Banja Luka in an enterprise called Veletekstil and afterwards as a travelling salesman for the same firm, and several years before the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina he worked as a travelling salesman for his own firm. He had some partners but I do not know them. 11 Q. Is it right that he was unable to continue in business as relationships between the states of the former Yugoslavia deteriorated? 14 A. Yes. 15 Q. The second son, your brother Mladen, is it right that he went to work and live in Germany? 17 A. Yes. 18 Q. When was that? 19 A. I think he left in 1973 or '74. He went to Munich and there he worked in the Siemens company. After that he worked in several private companies. All this went on until, I think, March of 1994. 23 Q. Did your brother Mladen keep up close contacts with the family in Kozarac? Did he visit them frequently or infrequently? 25 A. Yes, he came very frequently. From the first day he left for Germany, already after a year or a half, he would say that he would be coming back next year and this went on for 25 years. All people who went to Germany went in the belief that they would come back in two years time. He was very tied to our place. 3 Q. The third son and your other brother, Ljubomir, is it right that he went to live and work in Banja Luka? 5 A. Yes. When Mladen left for Germany -- I think this was in '73 or '74 -- he went to Banja Luka where our older brother had lived there before. He lived with him for a time. At the time -- at the same time he engaged in karate coaching. Afterwards he got a job in Cajavec and so on. 10 Q. We have heard that three of the sons of the Tadic family, Ljubomir, Mladen and yourself, have all been karate experts with black belt and having the fifth, fourth and third dan as grades amongst you, is that right? 14 A. The titles in karate are right, but to call us "experts", I think that is rather a broad term and perhaps it would be suited to Mladen who lived in a large west European centre. To a part, it could apply to Ljubomir who was among the more well-known competitors and coaches, but it could not be said of me, least of all of me, because I sort of went with them, but I did not have any special merits in that field. 21 Q. Did you coach karate within Kozarac? 22 A. Yes, I was an amateur coach of a club which was founded in 1981 in Kozarac based in the Kozarac elementary school. When I had time, I would conduct the coaching, but I was linked more to the Borac karate club in Banja Luka because in Kozarac I was working mainly with children aged seven to 12 mostly. There were no older members of the club. 28 Q. We heard from your brother, Ljubomir, that his club in Banja Luka was the Borac club. Was that a rather bigger scale karate club than what you were running in Kozarac? 3 A. The club in Kozarac was, one might say, insignificant for a long time. We were not even registered as a club because of the age group of the participants. We did not have any competitors. We mostly competed at the level of children, but the club in Banja Luka was a big one, a well-known one. It was founded by our older brother, Mladen, and when he left for Germany Ljubo continued to head the club and one could even make a living of that. This was not possible in Kozarac. This was just amateurism, recreation, nothing more. 12 Q. Did you take part in sporting competitions yourself, in karate competitions and matches, representing either your club or a local association? 15 A. For a time I did compete for the Borac karate club. There were several, one in Banja Luka, one in Belgrade and that is all. I was not a competitor. I mainly engaged in sport for my own satisfaction, and those who wanted to join with me. That is why I took part in the opening of the club in Kozarac. Many parents wanted this. It was an inexpensive sport. It did not require great funds. So that my participation in that sport in Kozarac was mainly educational, that is, I dealt with small children. 23 Q. How long did you run the karate classes at the school in Kozarac? 25 A. I officially led it. I was a registered coach, officially registered coach, but I had assistants from the first day. These were younger boys. I did not have so much time. From 1981 until I went to Libya I travelled to Banja Luka daily. I had to work in my company every working day and that is quite a distance from Kozarac. At first, I did not have my own car and even if I did it would be expensive to travel. I would get up at 4.35 a.m. and take a bus on the Prijedor to Banja Luka road at Kozarac at 5 a.m. We would get to Banja Luka at 6.00. I would get back at 6.00 or 7 p.m. the same day. So that I would spend two to three hours travelling, the rest working, and what time I had left I would be with my family. Occasionally, I would go to the club just to encourage them to develop the sport. I did not have time to dedicate myself to it. 12 Q. Did there come a time when you ceased running the club at Kozarac? 14 A. Yes. When I left for Libya in the previous few years several younger people had grown to competitor status, so there were people who wanted to continue the work of the club, and as of then I mostly -- I did not really engage in leading the club in Kozarac. 19 Q. It has been said in evidence that you were someone who would have been known in the area because you featured on the sports pages of the local newspapers such as Kozarski Vjesnik. Do you recollect being on the sports pages regularly? 23 A. No, there were often reports about my brothers, Mladen, Ljubomir. Mladen was one of the best known people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Yugoslavia as a master karate competitor, Ljubo too. But, as far as I am concerned, I do not remember such articles. There was no reason. I never won any competitions in Yugoslavia. I competed only a couple of times, so that there was no significance in that. Active sportsmen and competitors would have competitions at least twice a month. I did not have time for any such thing, and I did not look upon karate as a competitive sport. 5 Q. Did your brother Mladen represent Yugoslavia at international competitions? 7 A. I think he did several times at the international level in Hamburg. I do not know whether he was in Paris. I think he was. He did participate in several international competitions in Belgrade every year, in Sarajevo. He had a great deal of success, so did Ljubomir as a karatist. 12 Q. Did Ljubomir also represent Yugoslavia internationally? 13 A. Yes, for quite some time he competed together with representatives of a special karate style at various competitions in Europe and throughout Yugoslavia as well. 16 Q. Did you represent your country at international level? 17 A. No, not even at the Republican or inter-Republican level, no, never. 19 Q. What sort of level of competition were you in? 20 A. I think I participated in three competitions in all, as a competitor, but I participated as a coach and I took children to compete at these competitions. So I would be sitting there with the audience somewhere. My job was to take care of technical things, applications, travelling to and from the venue, giving advice such as coaches do. That was all. 26 Q. Did you continue with that work or did there come a time when your involvement in that aspect of karate ceased? 28 A. As I said, Kozarac did not have a competitive club for older members. Upon my return from Libya, I decided to go in for private business and dedicate myself to business and the family. So my sporting activities were reduced to recreational activities and contacts with friend. I had no participation in any public competitions from then. 6 Q. When you got married, did you live at the family home in Marsala Tita Street that we have seen photographs of during this case? 8 A. Yes. 9 Q. Did you always live there or did there come a time when you moved to live in another house or place in Kozarac? 11 A. I did not live there all the time. Around 1987 or '88 I lived in a house in Kalate Street in Kozarac also. 13 Q. Having lived there, did you eventually return to live with your parents back at the Tadic family home in Marsala Tita Street? 15 A. Yes, after our father died in 1989, somewhere around August, I returned to live in the family home in Marsala Tita Street in Kozarac. 18 Q. I would like you now to look at Exhibit 300 which is a photograph of the family home. If it could be put straightaway on the overhead projector? You can turn to the right. Thank you very much, Mr. Usher. As you know, we are very familiar in this courtroom now with this photograph and I want to run through this fairly quickly. We have been told that on the left-hand side is what is today a bar which originally was given to your brother Mladen by your father, is that right? 26 A. Yes. 27 Q. Next to that where the wider windows are, those are premises that are run by your brother Ljubomir, is that right? 1 A. [The witness indicated] Yes, at this time it is now a business space but it used to be a residence. 3 Q. The smaller window to the right of that is where your other brother Stojan was given a portion of the family home, is that right? 6 A. Yes. All these three parts had separate entrances from the outside. 8 Q. Originally, your parents' home was a single storey home where you and your other brothers were brought up, is that right? 10 A. Yes. It is this part. [The witness indicated] 11 Q. The extra floor on top of the ground floor, that was built at a later date, is that right? 13 A. Yes. This part here was built first and later on this one here, up here. 15 Q. Who lived in that upper storey above those ground floor sections that were eventually given to your brothers? 17 A. In the first period, when I first got married, I lived here. [The witness indicated]. Then I moved to Kalate and after the return I lived in this part here. [The witness indicated] Somewhere around 1990 I moved to this residential unit here. In 1990, this part was not completely finished inside and I completed it together with my wife and only then did we move in. 23 Q. We have heard about your father. He was an eminent person in Kozarac because of his distinction in the Second World War, is that right? 26 A. Yes. He was a well-known participant of World War II in 1941 and, not only that, because he was a well-known participant, he was also an honest and realistic man. He was 90 per cent handicapped because of the wounds he received during the war. That is on the one side. On the other side, he was also known as a man who was a very tolerant man from the World War II on regarding things national, and this is precisely why he moved to Kozarac in 1946 and continued to live there until his death. Throughout his life he continued to build this house, for one reason he wanted one -- he only needed one business unit but he wanted us all to come back and live there. He did not need all this space. 10 Q. As a former army officer, is it right that he was given a reasonable pension? 12 A. Yes, those were among the largest pensions in Yugoslavia at the time. It was a pension at a level almost like an average German salary of an average employee in Germany. So it was a good pension, and the very fact he was able to put all his children through school with that money and build a house talks about that. Plus, he had other privileges, ability to raise loans and then he had free trips to the coast. He never travelled by train. He would always take planes and he was a very sick man. 20 Q. The right-hand section of the family home that we see in that photograph was built at a later date, is that right? 22 A. Yes. 23 Q. Can you tell us when that right-hand section was built? 24 A. You think this part? 25 Q. No, on the ground floor which is slightly -- no, over on the right-hand side where the Nipon cafe was. 27 A. I think I showed it once. 28 Q. Yes. When was that built? 1 A. Construction of that part of the object was completed in 1990. The construction was started by -- I started about a month before my father's death in the summer of 1989. However, gathering of all the materials for this structure took much longer. From the first day when I went to Libya and when I opened the private business in Croatia, in the period between 1977 and '89 which means, 87, 89 when we lived in the Kalate Street, I was always in the field. I rarely ever got there, maybe two or three nights a month. I was always working in the field. I was with my company in Ljubljana, Zagreb, Belgrade, and my time was always on construction sites. It was a construction company. I am saying this because by working in the field I would come back to Kozarac every once in a while and gather the construction materials that I would need for construction of this structure, and so I started it in '89 and finished towards the end of 1990. 18 Q. Eventually, there came a stage when you opened a cafe in that side of the house, is that right? 20 A. Yes, towards the end of 1980 -- '90, that was in December and January. 22 Q. The upper part of that side of the house in red brick, was that built at a slightly later time? 24 A. No, it was built at the same time. The basic construction work was done by the end of 1990, but I was concentrating on the lower part for economic reasons so that I could start the business as soon as possible, calculating that if I use that money I could build the rest, but both were planned as a single business premises and the top part was never moved in. 2 Q. You completed the bottom part and then work on the upper section still remained to be finished, is that right? 4 A. Yes, in fact, I never stopped working. When I first opened my business, from the first day, I continued with the construction. I was gathering more materials. I was putting in installations. I was reckoning that until '92 or '93 I would open the other part of the premises and so that I could move my family, because the brother Ljubomir wanted to have this lower part where I was, that I was occupying at the time, turned into business space. 12 Q. The finance for that section of the house which you had your cafe built upon, did you obtain loans from various local people in order to contribute to the costs of the building? 15 A. The expense, the costs for this construction were very high. In any event, a lot of people helped me. My neighbours, friends, even relatives, would show up by themselves and offer to support that. Some offered labour, some offered financial aid, some without interest, some of the people came to my mother's. They knew that I was also building my residence where we wanted to move to. There were even people who offered it for their own economic interest. In that period, all dinar means were very difficult to raise. Adem Kahrimanovic is a good example. He had a lot of means in the local currency, dinars, but he could not raise them in value, and that in those circumstances we made an arrangement that he would give me about 10,000 deutschemarks at the time and I would give it back to him, but I needed to return it to him in dinar counter value. At that time I had to do it, it would be about 15,000 deutschemarks at a time by the time I returned it, so there were different ways in which people helped me and there were some economic reasonings in that. 5 Q. Did occasions occur when a number of local people would gather together and a sheep would be roasted and sections of the house would be built with a number of hands giving support? 8 A. Yes, that was a tradition in Kozarac. I do not know about the other parts, but Kozarac had that tradition. It was not a question whether you had money to pay people. It was a tradition which lasted, I do not know how long. When there were larger construction works, if you had to put the roof or put a concrete plate on top, then all neighbours would come over. I remember when there were cases when two brothers, they were not -- they did not have a good relationship, they did not even have a contact, even though they were relatives, but the family members would always go there, regardless. It was an old tradition in those parts. The host -- it was an unwritten rule -- would either put a pig on a spit and they would give out the drinks, and it was not material benefit, it was a tradition. 22 Q. What time did your cafe start to trade and you receive customers from within Kozarac? 24 A. In December 1990 I started -- I started trading in this cafe Nipon. 26 Q. In that period until the conflict in May 1992, was it a successful business? 28 A. Yes, I thought that it was successful. I thought it was a success. I never worked as a waiter there at any time. I was the owner of the cafe and I mostly did other jobs which was supplying and then dealing with the tax authorities and local administration, pay rolls and such, but I thought that it was rather successful. 6 Q. Was it a place that was particularly popular with the youngsters in Kozarac? 8 A. Yes, mostly the young people. I think that the average age of my patrons was between 14 and 18. However, the older people from the centre used to come early for coffee. They were older people and it was expresso Italian coffee and it was very high quality, and I would sit with them and then they would go on their business and I on my own. But, otherwise, when the dusk fell, I had the youth. Sometimes I was the oldest person who would walk in there, and sometimes I would not stay there very much. I had younger waiters, young men and women. It was for the youth. There were no folk music there which was what people mostly listened to in Bosnia. I was getting music cassettes from abroad, from my brother or somebody else, so it was mostly disco or music from abroad. This is what they were interested in, the youth there. 22 Q. It is right that your ethnic background is described as being Serbian, is that right? 24 A. I do not know. I am a Serb. 25 Q. As a Serb opening a coffee bar in Kozarac at this time, did you employ people of different ethnic backgrounds to work there with you? 28 A. Yes. The whole time while the business was open, I never had 1 more than two waiters. However, one was always a Muslim, the 2 entire time. The other one could have been any other 3 nationality, but one waiter would always be a Muslim. I did 4 that on advice, for the most part, of my neighbours who were 5 natives there. It was reasoning that I would not want to create 6 an impression that this was a Serb cafe. It was for all the 7 people of Kozarac, and mostly Muslims went there, if that is 8 what you are asking about their national background. As far as I could notice, I never polemicized about 10 that and I never kept any statistics who was coming. But, since 11 I was born in Kozarac, I lived there, 98 per cent of people 12 there were Muslim. Many Serbs, I do not know why, but they were 13 not coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Given the costs that were involved in building these premises 15 and running them, could your business have been successful if it 16 had only restricted those who were welcome there to being those 17 only of Serbian background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, not even -- I can count how many Serbs came, maybe seven 19 or eight. Sometimes it was a cafe -- there were always 100 or 20 sometimes over 200 people there every night, I cannot tell, 21 because I did the finances, I know what the turnover was there, 22 how much beverages had been used. So I know that my average was 23 between 100 and 200, and in Kozarac you did not have enough 24 Serbs in that period. Especially in 1991, a lot of Serbs and 25 young men who were potential patrons were in different war zones 26 around Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: With the cafe running, were you able to repay the loans that you 28 had obtained from some of the local people? 1 A. I do not know if you understood me well. Every once in a while I would get money, but I would also loan money to others. Of course, I would always return money. There were no -- it was my business was always clean that way, but it would happen that one of either Sefik Arnautovic or Adil Jakupovic -- in Yugoslavia, you always had a problem with foreign currency, and the dinar would lose about 30 per cent of the value at a time. Often, people would come and ask one, two or 3,000 deutschemarks at a time. That would be my daily intake and they needed it for a man who was exchanging 20 or 30,000 marks for them, and then they would give me the counter value in dinars the next day. So this is how we exchanged, so there was no problem there. But whether I could keep in business if my patrons were only Serbs, that is a silly question; you could not even think about that. It is well-known the structure of the population in Kozarac, plus I never thought of who would be my patrons in my cafe. 18 Q. Just to clear up one matter, although the dinar was the official currency in the former Yugoslavia, would it be right to say that a lot of business was really done with deutschemarks? 21 A. Yes, mostly. 22 Q. The other section of the house that your brother Ljubomir had given to him, did that open as business premises as well? 24 A. Precisely, because Ljubo saw that my business is taking off and it was successful, I suggested to him that he should do something similar and I suggested I know that he was -- that my neighbour, Adil Jakupovic, was in a dilemma. He said, "How is that possible?" He did not want to take that risk to open up a private business. I know that he often told me later that because of my advice he took that road and that was after me. So, also Ljubo, because of my suggestions, opened a private business in that former residential part of our old family house. He opened it, I think it was somewhere 15, 20 days before the war started. 7 Q. What business did he open there? 8 A. His business was linked to the brewery in Banja Luka. He made a business arrangement. They would ship the goods to him on a regular basis. He would distribute it. He would have a certain percentage from distribution. So that was wholesale, so he was distributing wholesale. So it was not a bottle or two or three but larger quantities and through that, and that was the practice in the Prijedor municipality. From such distribution centres others would supply. For instance, if I wanted some beverages, I would buy with him, of course, or somebody else because it was much cheaper. It was like a factory price. It was as if you bought it in Banja Luka. 19 Q. He described it as a beer discount store. Would that be a correct description? 21 A. Yes, I think that that was the official title. He should know that. 23 Q. Did he also sell soft drinks there? 24 A. Yes. 25 Q. Was his business in that 21 days or so before the war started in Kozarac successful in that short period? 27 A. Yes, very successful. 28 Q. Did it look as though that was a business, if allowed to continue, would have been something that would have continued to have been successful in Kozarac? 3 A. Yes, that is certain. I had some acquaintances in Prijedor who in a short period of time became rich doing this kind of business. I think it was an excellent business. I think it was better than the one I had. 7 MR. KAY: Your Honour, that looks to be an appropriate moment. 8 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. 9 (4.00 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 11 (4.20 p.m.) 12 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Kay, you may begin. 13 MR. KAY: Thank you, your Honour. 14 Q. I would like to ask you some questions now about your relationships with the other residents of Kozarac. Were you on friendly terms with most people there? 17 A. Yes. 18 Q. Were you a person who mixed with people from Croatian backgrounds, Muslims ---- 20 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Excuse me one moment, Mr. Kay. I am just checking to see if there is sound going to the gallery. Yes, it is coming through now. I am sorry, Mr. Kay. 23 MR. KAY: That is all right, your Honour. I will just start the last question again. [To the witness]: Were you someone who mixed with people who were Croats or Muslims or other ethnic backgrounds within Kozarac? 27 A. Yes. I did not make any differences in terms of ethnic origin. That was how our father brought us up, both me and my other brothers. I paid no attention. I may have had friends of Serb nationality, but most of my friends were Muslims and Croats. 3 Q. Living within Kozarac, would it have been difficult for you to restrict yourself to friendships with only Serbian people? 5 A. First of all, it is hard to answer that question, because there were few Serbs of my generation. I do not think anyone -- in my childhood, in elementary school, they were all Muslims. I did not have a Serb friend. 9 Q. In the ---- 10 A. I cannot remember a single Serb with whom I was close, that we used to visit each other at home. No, I cannot remember a single one. 13 Q. Did that present you with any particular problems, any particular difficulty, in life or was it something that was just natural and you were able to deal with? 16 A. I simply did not pay attention to such things. The people I was friendly with also, we never talked about such things. We never had any polemics. That was how I was brought up, as I said, me and my brothers. I also, when we are talking about this, let me add I was not christened. We are not religious people. We did not celebrate religious feasts. We celebrated the state holidays of the former Yugoslavia which were the same for all ethnic groups. There was no difference. I do not know how he declared himself officially, but I do not remember myself or any of my friends ever discussing ethnic differences. This was something we simply did not pay any attention to. 28 Q. Did your cafe bar in the months just before the conflict in 1 Kozarac become a place that was a focus, a centre, for those who 2 were of Serbian background who had returned from the front, who 3 had been fighting in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think it was ever a centre for one particular 5 ethnic group, particularly not the military. The military would 6 go to cafes where good quality food was being served, not just 7 drinks. In those days the soldiers were well paid in '91. As 8 I said earlier, my cafe was a place where the young people would 9 come. I cannot say that occasionally older people did not 11 come by, they did, but only rarely. They spent a short time 12 there. They did not enjoy disco music. They were not 13 interested in pop songs. They were interested in the songs 14 glorifying nationalist leaders, and my cafe was never a meeting 15 place for such guests. Sometimes people from the Territorial Defence would 17 drop in, members of the JNA perhaps, but this was not a 18 gathering place that was happening in other restaurants or cafes 19 where food was being served, Neira, Red Roses. The guests were 20 mostly people who had plenty of money, who were ready to spend 21 it on food. My guests were young men and women who had pocket 22 money given by their parents to spend that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You mentioned Neira and Red Roses, were they other cafes in 24 Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These two that I mentioned, they are not cafes, they are 26 restaurants, and I mentioned them because that was where food 27 was served. In cafes, food was not served, as a rule. There 28 were other cafes, but the army, the military, would mainly go to these two restaurants. I never heard that there were any problems there either. I went there rarely, but whenever I did, it was packed to capacity with guests with various insignia of all kinds. 5 Q. We have heard of a friendship you had with a man called Emir Karabasic. When did you first meet him? 7 A. I met Emir Karabasic in 1980 or '81, when I became leader of the karate club in Kozarac. I first met his younger brother, Esmir, and then Emir. I do not know, but later we found out that my father and his grandfather had somehow close relations. They were both participants in the Second World War and had very good and close relations, and those relationships between the elders were always passed on to the younger generations. Emir Karabasic graduated secondary school in Sarajevo. He returned to the Prijedor municipality. He worked at a time in Prijedor. Then he worked in Omarska for four or five times, then for a time in Ljubija. That is it, as much as I know. 18 Q. The work you described, was that Emir Karabasic working as a police officer? 20 A. Yes. 21 Q. We saw a photograph when your wife gave evidence. Perhaps D71 could be put on the overhead projector, so that it is made clear? Perhaps Miss Sutherland may be able to assist? I know she can work the machine. Thank you. We see there a photograph of the family on holiday apparently taken by you, is that right? 26 A. Yes. 27 Q. That is your wife and your eldest daughter Valentina with your eldest brother Stojan, is that right? 1 A. Yes. 2 Q. Emir is sitting on the towels behind your wife, is that right? 3 A. Yes. 4 Q. So, your friendship with him was a friendship where you went on holiday together? 6 A. Our friendship was much greater than many are aware of. Relations between me and this older brother, for instance, were blood relationships, but with Karabasic and some of my great friends, we would visit each other, spend the night, eat at each other's houses, his problems were mine and my problems were his. They were our common problems. He was like a brother to me, and I think he considered me the same. This was a photograph when we went to the seaside together. It was taken in Medulin, near Pula, in Croatia. I think we spent about three weeks together at the seaside. I do not know what else I could say, but we slept in the same room. We shared the same room. 17 Q. What would the date of that holiday have been? 18 A. I think this was taken in 1983. We went to the seaside together several times. This was not the first time. We would go to Belgrade, to various places. It is difficult to remember each of those trips, but any family festivity or reunion at my home could not take place without him and his wife attending. They knew -- he knew all my friends in Banja Luka, in Prijedor. He was like a member of the family. Paolo and Vesna, when they would come to Banja Luka, would say, "Invite Karabasic" and I would go and call him because we could not have any get together without him. We were together in sports too, but it was not at the level that people may think. His brother was a much better karatist, but he and I were friends. We were much closer otherwise, not in sports. On a Saturday morning, he would come at 5 o'clock and we would run towards Mount Kozara jogging, then we would come back and we had some wonderful times together. 6 Q. Your wife said that he was a single man who had many girlfriends. Did he have a wife? Was he married or did he have a steady girlfriend? 9 A. It is hard to say. As in my case I got married, but not officially. The moment we made our vows to each other, we considered ourselves married. We did not consider a paper to be important. Anyway, in Yugoslavia any extra marital community had equal status as an official marriage. Emir Karabasic was in a similar situation. He did have a wife, but in 1990 he lost a baby upon delivery. I was in Banja Luka then. I was staying with my friends, Selcek(?). We had a road accident so we went back to Banja Luka. This was a terrible blow for him and for me, of course. After that, the relationship between him and his wife at the time cooled, so that afterwards one could say he was married or he was not. The death of the baby contributed to the collapse of that union. That is why probably my wife thought that he was sometimes married, sometimes not. 24 Q. When your father Ostoja died, was he one of the bearers of the coffin at your father's funeral? 26 A. Yes. Yes. 27 Q. Who were the other bearers of your father's coffin? 28 A. Mostly friends, my brothers, among others, Vercek Paolo, my 1 friend from Banja Luka. I will never forget it. We bathed my 2 father when he died. Karabasic carried him out. They were -- 3 we were always at each other's side when we were in difficulty 4 and when we were enjoying ourselves. Karabasic was there all 5 the time, not just he, but many other of my friends and 6 neighbours. My friends from elementary school, they came to 7 attend the funeral from various parts of Yugoslavia, not just 8 those living there at the time. In our parts, funerals, 9 weddings, are a time to show respect towards one's neighbours 10 and it is something one remembers, one never forgets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before the conflict in Kozarac on 24th May 1992, how would you 12 describe your friendship with Emir Karabasic at that stage, at 13 that point of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the beginning -- at the end of 1991, at the beginning of 15 1992, Emir Karabasic had many personal problems. In the middle 16 of 1989 he was working as a policeman in Omarska for four years 17 by then and I was familiar with all of his problems. At that 18 time, he led a karate group in Lamovita and Omarska. He spent 19 many years living and working there, and I do not know the 20 reasons, but for six months Karabasic was suspended as a 21 policeman at the end of '91/beginning of '92, and he immediately 22 appealed to me and my brother to try and help him to move to 23 Banja Luka or to some other town. I do not know the real reasons why he was suspended as 25 a policeman, but I know that he was laid off for six months. He 26 fought for that job because he always said that was the only 27 thing he knew how to do. My relationship towards him did not 28 change, but he was very busy with his own personal problems. I do not know whether they had to do with Omarska or Kozarac. Many of his colleagues did not like him. They reported against him. They claimed that he acted contrary to the policemen's code. He was an honest policeman on duty, and when he was off duty he was like anybody else who liked company. Probably some of his colleagues did not like this and they complained against him. It happened in Omarska and in Kozarac too. They would go to higher level authorities to report him. Our relationships at the time did not change particularly, but we did not see each other so often because of those personal problems. I remember that he came on several occasions to see me and my wife. Whenever he passed by, he would drop in. He would often bring cevapcici, minced meatballs. Maybe he had problems because he was a great friend of mine, I do not know really, but in any case we did not see each other very often then. I attributed this to the problems that he was having in the police because he often told me about them. 20 Q. He was of Muslim ethnic background, is that right? 21 A. Yes, he was a Muslim but he considered himself a Yugoslav, a typical Yugoslav. 23 Q. As a policeman working in Omarska, that would have been him working within a particular village that had a concentration of Serbian people and Serbian policemen within the town, would that be right? 27 A. Yes, Karabasic worked in Ormaska for four or five years. 28 Q. Omarska, unlike Kozarac, was a particular area that had a concentration of Serbian people? 2 A. It was similar to Kozarac in the sense that in Kozarac there was a larger percentage of Muslims and in Omarska there was a much larger percentage of Serbs. 5 Q. You said that your relationship changed between the two of you, but was there any animosity, was there any dislike, or was it that he had problems at that particular time and your friendship for that period was not based upon the same previous friendship that you had had before? 10 A. I still think that even at the time that he was my best friend and I his. Our relationships did not change particularly. As I said, maybe the atmosphere in those parts had changed and it required everyone to take care of himself. I did not have much time to roam around. I did not dare to as I did before; I spent most of my time at home or in my cafe or visiting family in Banja Luka, and Karabasic too was working in Ljubija at that time. This is another part of the municipality of Prijedor. But our relationships did not change. We would always meet, talk about all kinds of things. We just did not see each other so often because out of technical reasons this was no longer possible. Karabasic worked in Omarska. We would see each other through sport, and then he moved to Ljubija. Sports activities died down. Ljubija was quite far away, but our relationship did not change. I know when his brother died in a traffic accident I attended the funeral. We talked. I know I was upset. This was just a few months before the war. 27 Q. Did he ever serve in Kozarac before the war -- now I am just talking about in 1992 -- as a policeman in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think so. We never talked about it, about the police 2 too much, and I am not sure, to be perfectly honest. Our 3 conversation was usually about private problems, sports or 4 family relations, what happened within my family and my friends 5 and his friends. That was our -- that was our conversation. We 6 never had special conversations about my business and he about 7 his own. All our conversations were unofficial in character. 8 It was private in nature, like with a family member, we never 9 polemicized much about anything, but I do not think he worked in 10 Kozarac, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said in answer to an earlier question that the atmosphere 12 had changed in the area. Can you, as far as you are concerned, 13 give a time when it was detectable that the atmosphere in 14 Kozarac had changed from what it had been in the old days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the atmosphere in Kozarac was no different from the 16 one that was around in all of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I do not 17 know exactly when this Assembly was constituted, the multi-party 18 one, but I remember that those proceedings were televised, that 19 people were talking among themselves. They had fears. The 20 conflicts in Sarajevo somehow, they were spreading to other 21 parts. The conflicts that were there, they were frightening 22 people, if you look from that propaganda angle. On the other hand, the war in Croatia was a fact, and 24 from day-to-day you could see that it was moving towards 25 Bosnia. It was a fact with which we lived. We were all fearing 26 that it would spill over into Bosnia, and the President there 27 said that they would do anything to move the war into Bosnia 28 and, in essence, this is what actually happened. People lived in fear. There was a general fear. 2 Q. Did there come a time when you, in fact, received a threatening letter whilst you were in Kozarac? 4 A. Yes, that happened in August of 1990, around the time of the death of my father. 6 Q. It has been suggested by some witnesses that were called at an earlier stage in the proceedings that either you or your wife had written this letter as some sort of gesture, is that right? 9 A. No. Not at all, neither myself nor my wife wrote this, nor do I know who wrote this. I do not know who wrote this letter. I received that letter. It is a fact, it happened. It can happen to anybody. I never hid that -- for the first few days I did hide. I did not want anybody to know in the family. Then I thought about it and I felt, somehow my conscience woke up and if something did happen I would have felt guilty that I did not say about that, and those threats were also directed not only at me but my mother, my wife and I lived in Kozarac at the time with my mother and my wife and two children, and I was afraid for their security. At that time when it was not right for me to hide, then I showed it to my wife and my mother and I called my brothers to ask them what to do and I wanted to leave. However, I talked to my neighbours who were Muslims and members of SDA Party, and they said, not to pay any attention to that, that they would support me, that there was no problem. I asked the veterans' union representative and I invited him to my house and we talked, and I talked to Mr. Kahrimanovic with Adil Jakupovic. I talked to a lot of my neighbours and I wanted to 2 find a real solution because it would not have been fair of me 3 to have left a place as if I was expelled. I did not want 4 that. The only thing I could do was I turned the letter over to 5 the police in Prijedor, and I did not want something to happen 6 and I did not -- I had not done something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In August 1990 when you received that letter, had you had any 8 indications before that date that certain people might be 9 viewing you with animosity or dislike?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will tell you. After my father's death and especially after 11 I decided to build the business premises in Kozarac when it was 12 visible that I would open this cafe, because before I was 13 thinking I wanted to go abroad, that was my long time wish, but 14 I never succeeded for a number of years. Then I decided to 15 continue my life in Kozarac and then I decided to invest 16 everything I had into that. I do not know. Since I started building this cafe, some things 18 started. There were some things that were happening that 19 reminded me that there were some people there who did not want 20 me to continue my life there. To date, I do not know who it 21 was. I think it could have been the competition of other cafe 22 owners. I do not think it was a movement or anything. 23 I thought it about it for a long time. Maybe somebody 24 interpreted it that way. I think that that was a bit false, this letter. I did 26 not -- I thought it was a provocation. It could have been done 27 by anybody. After all, it could have been done by Serbs. It 28 was all possible. I did not -- I could not find out a solution 1 about it. As far as the relationships are concerned later on, 3 sometimes there were phone threats to my daughter or my wife. 4 Once I picked up that phone and I talked to this person who had 5 called, and it seemed silly to me, but my daughter was afraid 6 and so my wife. I did not pay much attention to it, but 7 especially through the accent, I could figure out it was nobody 8 from that area. I thought it was somebody from abroad. It was 9 not an accent of a person who lives in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It 10 was a female and it was ridiculous, what the voice was saying, 11 and it effected my family much more than it did me. I did not 12 speak about it much to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this time from 1990 was there suddenly more political 14 activity within Kozarac and the area of Prijedor generally? 15 Were people identifying themselves for the first time with 16 political parties in a way that they had never experienced 17 before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say that was the case. I think from the very 19 beginning of the creation of the national parties, for instance, 20 SDA, SDS, HDZ, those parties were representing themselves in 21 public as if they were to co-operate in the future, that the 22 main enemy was the former communist system, that that was their 23 priority. All parties proclaimed that, both the nationalist 24 ones and the others, and they were leaving an impression among 25 common people that the important thing was to defeat communism 26 and their relationships would be splendid; as if in the former 27 system the nations did not have their representatives and now 28 they would represent them, especially HDZ and SDS and SDA. That is how people also thought. So it was generally a movement. In the beginning it did not seem to me like a party organisation. There were movements, one can say, and the Croats mostly joined HDZ and the Serbs SDS and Muslims to the SDA. That is how it started. The relations among people and this taking memberships in these parties did not cause discord among common people. I do not know a single case when people came into a conflict because one was a member of HDZ or SDS or SDA. There were no such cases. I do not know any of these parties had platforms that would hurt -- be hurtful to other nations. I do not know about that. 12 Q. When did you join the SDS? 13 A. In 1990. 14 Q. Was that before or after you had received that letter? 15 A. That was later. Not only after I received the letter, but several months later it turned out that the investigation that allegedly was conducted was fruitless. Then there were several additional phone calls and threats, and my wife insisted that we had to take some shelter with some side. Then we went to Prijedor to the health centre and that Dragoje Musac(?) was working there. He said that they would take us in and so we became members, my wife, myself and my brother. 23 Q. The Prosecution in this case have quoted from a document that you wrote saying that you were one of the first members of the SDS in the Prijedor region. Do you know if that is right? 26 A. Theoretically, that was impossible. Up until the establishment of the local committee of the party, I was not a member of any SDS or HDZ or SDA. You have to be a member of this local committee, go to meetings and be part of the committee. Membership of a party is nothing. It would be almost like an honorary membership. I was not a member of any local committee. There was no local committee, and I could not have attended meetings in Prijedor in any local committee. That was the procedure. So there was no dilemma there. 7 Q. In November 1991, there was a plebiscite held for Serbian people. Is it right that you conducted that plebiscite on behalf of the SDS in Kozarac? 10 A. I think that that is not the right definition. 11 Q. Perhaps then you can ---- 12 A. That reflects the real situation. The fact of the matter is that probably the SDS was the initiator of the plebiscite. . I think that the initiative for the plebescite came from the SDS. However, all this was conducted through the Local Assembly in Prijedor. There was a Commission of the Municipal Assembly that was in charge to organise the plebescite. I do not know what the procedure was to be followed at the municipal level, the party and the Municipal Assembly, but the party itself could not have organised such a plebiscite. The party could table it, but there is a commission for plebiscite. Non-partisan members had to be appointed and I think that the control of this plebiscite, one of the people who controlled it was Jovan Vukoje and this man was not a member of the SDS. I think he was a socialist or something. 26 Q. If we could have a look at Exhibit 146 and at the same time if you could pull out 147. If 146 could be put on the monitor. If you could put the English version on the monitor and give the defendant the copy in his own language. Thank you very much. I hope that can be read by everyone. This document here is the decision on the appointment of voting officials for the plebiscite in the area of Kozarac, Vidovici, and you were to be the President of the voting officials. The document is actually dated 8th November 1991 and signed by Dragan Savanovic. Can you tell us how it was that you came about to be appointed with this position and this responsibility? Whose decision was it? 9 A. First of all, I would like to say that at the top of the document here it is clearly stated that the organiser of this was commissioned, a municipal plebiscite commission, that is what I said. 13 Q. Is that a municipal plebescite commission of Prijedor or elsewhere? 15 A. Exactly as I said. It is the municipal commission that was appointed by the Municipal Assembly. I do not know the procedure, but I assume that the suggestion came from the SDS within the Assembly, and then based on that suggestion this commission was established who took over the responsibility for this plebiscite, the same way for the referendum that the SDA initiated. They could not do themselves, so it was all down at the municipal level. Again, a commission was formed that was put in charge of it. 24 Q. Were you approached by someone beforehand and asked if you would undertake this responsibility, or were you just notified in some way that you would be expected to undertake this responsibility? 27 A. I remember exactly how it took place. At that time in Kozarac, as in other places in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were some multi-party governments. There were a few representatives of different parties in this Executive Committee. The SDS was represented by Zivko Kos from the village of Balte, Babici or Balte, I do not know exactly. At that time both Balte and Babici were belonging to the Local Commune of Kozarac. As far as I know, they already had previously formed SDS committees there. Based on that Zivko Kos who was a member of the Council of Local Commune of Kozarac, at that time he visited me and asked me whether I would undertake with some people to organise this plebiscite at voting station 36 which was in Vidovici. Here it states clearly that this is voting station 36. In the Local Commune in Kozarac there were at least five or six such polling stations, so this would be one of them. 14 Q. This document refers to polling place No. 36 in Vidovici. Were there other such documents such as this that indicated other polling places for this plebiscite? 17 A. Here is mentioned Kozarac, Vidovici, as you can see, but mostly it was planned that the plebiscite would be held in the village of Vidovici which has seven families living there. Because of that it was not practical for them to go to Kamicani, to another place, so that is why it had been suggested that this polling station be formed there. It was assumed that there were only a few families of Serb background that lived there. So it was expected that there would not be many votes. 25 Q. So was your responsibility as the President of the voting officials for the plebiscite also concerned with the other polling stations around Kozarac? 28 A. No. This was only for the polling station 36, but not for Kozarac. It is only for the village of Vidovici. However, we organised that in an office that was in the churchyard in Kozarac. The only reason for that was because there were no other communal objects, and it would not have been right to hold the plebiscite in a private house. So we went to this place. 6 Q. So would it be right to say that Vidovici in fact did not have a polling place No. 36 on plebiscite day? 8 A. Correct. Another reason for holding this in the centre of Kozarac, it seemed to me that to organise a plebiscite in a Serb village would not be right in Kozarac, since I lived in the centre of Kozarac. It seemed to me to be like some kind of clandestine voting. It would not have been fair. That was one of the reasons why we decided that the plebiscite take place in Kozarac. It would be questionable to hold the voting in a single ethnic group, place. I did not think it was right. 16 Q. Can we look now at Exhibit 147. Could the Serbo-Croatian version be put in front of the defendant and the English version on the monitor. This is headed as the Minutes of the Election Committee for the day of the plebiscite on 9th November. I think you have already told us that this took place actually in the Serbian Orthodox church office in Kozarac, that is right, is it not? 23 A. Not in the church, but an office in the churchyard. 24 Q. Yes, that is what I meant. If the English version can now be pushed further up the monitor, please, so we have the bottom half of the page fully on display. Thank you very much. This is a record of the numbers of people who voted. Was this a particular responsibility of checking the ballot for the day by you and your committee? 2 A. It was not just me that had to do that. I was President of the commission who had to supervise to make sure that everything was in order, but since it lasted two days many people took turns, not just those on the list; there were many others who took turns. After the voting we acted according to the procedure. There was a document indicating the actual procedure for packing and counting the ballots. They had to be packed and then after a certain time sent to the Municipal Assembly in Prijedor. They were not sent to party headquarters, but to the Municipal Assembly and its commission responsible for organising the plebiscite in the municipality of Prijedor. 13 Q. At this time in November 1991 were you someone who had read a great deal of the political text, other documents that were issued by the party of the SDS? 16 A. I never read anything linked to the SDS or to any other party. In the first place, I had no access to the documents of the SDS party. I was not a member of any local committee, as I said, so I do not see how I could have participated in any such activities. I am not aware of any publications made nor did I ever receive any such documentation. 22 Q. Was the scale of the SDS in Kozarac a very small scale operation without a great deal of organisation? 24 A. There was no SDS in Kozarac until 1992. This is quite clear. Furthermore, many people who were members of the SDS did not proclaim their affiliation in public. I personally did not know who was a member, nor did many know that I was a member. I paid membership fees once and never again. Then I lost my little booklet, membership booklet. So my membership in the SDS in that period was quite insignificant. They must have kept a record in Prijedor of members and I was on that record, on that register, but there was no SDS active in Kozarac at the time. 5 Q. We know that in August 1992 you eventually became the President of the SDS in Kozarac. I am not now concerned with that period, but the period before the conflict. Did you have any official position within the party before the conflict started in Kozarac? 10 A. I told you that until the conflict started in 1992 there was no local SDS committee in Kozarac, officially or unofficially. As far as I am aware, the closest local committee of the SDS was in Jaruge or Babici or somewhere there, but in the centre of Kozarac where I lived there was no SDS local committee registered, nor were any meetings of the SDS party held. Officially the local committee of the SDS was registered in December 1992. That is quite evident. 18 Q. At this time before the conflict in May 1992, did you attend any political assemblies in Prijedor which would have involved the SDS? Did you attend any of their meetings? 21 A. I apologise, could you please repeat the period you are referring to? 23 Q. Before the conflict in Kozarac did you attend any of the meetings of the SDS in Prijedor? 25 A. No, I never attended any meeting of the SDS. It could not have happened. I do not know how to explain it to you. If you were not a member of a local committee you could not attend such a meeting. I know this because the procedure for attending meetings was the same procedure as existed during the communist system. There were local organisations of the League of Communists and these local organisations had a list of members. People were called you out and it was their duty to attend those meetings. Several absences without justification would entail dismissal from the party. Another obligation was to pay membership fees. That was one of the most important duties. If you were irregular in your payment of fees you would be deleted from the register. I am saying this because I think that a similar procedure existed in all other parties. I was not a member of any local committee, and if I wanted to I could not attend such meetings. Every member could attend assembly meetings of the Serbian Democratic Party that were held once a year, but I did not attend ever such assemblies either. 15 Q. Did you have high contacts within the SDS party, with people who were officials? 17 A. I think that the highest official I knew was called Zivko Kos, that is as much as I knew, but I did not have special contacts with other people. Of course, I learnt from the media who was President of the party, the SDS party, but I did not have any special relationships with any of them. I know from the time the parties were formed that the relations among the party leaders were good. Then later I do not know what happened with those relations. 25 Q. Did they supply you as an individual with any information as to what they were doing, what they were planning? 27 A. No. No, I did not even have a statute. I assume there must have existed a statute of the party. I do not know. I am not aware of it. However, no one ever showed it to me or read from it to me. I do not know what the programme of those political parties were, any of the parties. I was not really interested to be quite frank. 5 Q. When the takeover of Prijedor took place on 29th April 1992 and the organs of power within Prijedor were subject to the control of the SDS, were you aware of that event before it happened? 8 A. No. I heard of it for the first time I think it was a Thursday. I remember hearing about it from my neighbours. The first to tell me was Adil Jakupovic. A large number of people from Kozarac were turned back from their way to work. They were turned back to Kozarac. They simply could not go to work on that day and that is when I heard from them for the first time that there had been a takeover of power, that relations had become strained. I do not know the reason, but I know for sure that many were turned back. They told me that they had been turned back from entering Prijedor. I saw lots of people going by and I enquired and many neighbours told me this. I never listened to the radio, but I heard about it from the neighbours that I saw. 21 Q. Were you in Prijedor on that day of 29th April? Did you take any part in taking over the institutions of the town either on that day or on the days afterwards? 24 A. No. 25 Q. Did anyone invite you to take part in the takeover of the institutions within Prijedor on that day or the days immediately following? 28 A. No. I do not see why. What could I have done? What could I have helped? In what way could I have helped? I do not think the idea had ever struck anyone. There was no point, no reason. 3 Q. When that takeover occurred, what effect did it have on the people within a town such as Kozarac? 5 A. People did feel upset. I spoke to many neighbours then. I think it was done in an unfair manner. People were surprised, more perhaps because those political parties ever since their foundation had managed to convince the average citizen that they were co-operating, that there was not any chance of anything happening. They kept advocating the idea that what was most important was to overcome the communist system. There was a general euphoria and you could frequently see people sitting together belonging to different parties, drinking and saying, "We have defeated communism". Ordinary people were not aware of where it was all leading. 16 Q. Before that takeover took place on 29th April, had your family left Kozarac for any substantial period of time to live elsewhere? 19 A. Yes, on April 1st. 20 Q. Why was that on April 1st? 21 A. Several months before that, maybe ever since March, people were getting armed. After the last few months people would not even hide their weapons. They would walk in the streets armed and there was general chaos. The more serious people would not carry weapons in public, but the younger generations would not conceal their weapons. They were getting organised in a sense. I know there were many lists of who would go to which shelter. They were listing buildings. Nobody informed me about anything, 1 I was never invited. I simply felt isolated in that period. 2 Furthermore, I noticed that anyone who had anywhere to go had 3 left, particularly those who had a member of the family abroad, 4 Germany or Slovenia. People were leaving en masse and it was 5 very difficult to get a bus ticket at the time. Those from 6 Banja Luka going to Belgrade were full too. Whoever had 7 anywhere to go went. I simply had no other place to go to. So 8 I sent my family. My wife arranged with a friend of hers that 9 they go to Sanski Most. People were on the move. People were 10 leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why were weapons and arms suddenly being visible and able to be 12 seen in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the real answer to that question. Perhaps if 14 I look back at all that happened, I think that everything that 15 was happening in Sarajevo created fear in people. The war in 16 Croatia was getting closer. People felt scared. They feared 17 one another. Then there were groups that emerged, people with a 18 criminal past, for example, Suljo Kusuran who had served time in 19 prison for many years on the Serb side. There were some 20 extremists in Prijedor too and these groups created this fear 21 among people. They would fire shots. They would act in an 22 unruly manner. I knew that people would sell a car to buy a 23 rifle. They would build dug-outs next to their homes. That 24 I could understand because people remembered the last war and 25 the weapons were probably because they feared for their family, 26 but to carry weapons, that was most unpleasant to see, 27 particularly in an environment in which there were five or six 28 families that were Serb in my street, the street I was living in. I think my house was the only Serb house. So that was one of the reasons why I sent my family to Sanski Most. 3 MR. KAY: Your Honour, that is a convenient moment. 4 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Wladimiroff, I have been told that you wish that the Trial Chamber meet on Monday? 6 MR. WLADIMIROFF: That is right, your Honour. 7 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: We are at your disposal. 8 MR. WLADIMIROFF: Thank you very much. 9 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: It might be better. You will need that time to complete your witnesses, will you not? Do you think you will finish by Tuesday? 12 MR. WLADIMIROFF: We will aim to do that, but it would be very helpful if we can sit on Monday indeed. 14 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Niemann, I will ask if there is any objection. Is there any? 16 MR. NIEMANN: No, your Honour. 17 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Very good, then we will. We did discuss the closing arguments. The Trial Chamber has decided that the only date I suppose that will fit with both of the schedules of the Prosecutor and the Defence, since you are not available on 14th (and then the courtroom is being used by the other Chamber on 19th and 20th) would be November 25th. So we want the closing arguments to begin on Monday, November 25th at 10 a.m. If you wish to submit written submissions then those should be filed by November 20th. As we have indicated, it would be very helpful to us in either the written submissions or orally that you give references and charts or outlines, however you want to do it. In the written submission, of course, you will need to discuss 1 the facts and how they relate to the law, the elements. Do not 2 forget about Article 7(1). That was not mentioned in either of 3 the pretrial briefs. Do not forget about the nature of the 4 conflict, internationality. Perhaps we can talk more about it, but I wanted to 6 give those dates, November 25th at 10 a.m. for the closing 7 arguments. Written submissions are to be filed on 20th. We 8 will adjourn until Monday at 10 a.m. (5.30 p.m.).
